accepted.question_text: Do short-baseline and other neutrino anomalies—LSND and MiniBooNE antimuon-to-antielectron appearance, reactor antineutrino disappearance, gallium calibration deficits, possible differences between neutrino and antineutrino oscillations, low-energy MiniBooNE excesses, possible seasonal variations, and OPERA's reported superluminal muon-neutrino velocity—represent real physics beyond standard three-flavour neutrino oscillations, and if so can a single theory explain them quantitatively, for example by sterile neutrinos, CPT violation, or nonstandard matter interactions, while satisfying the existing oscillation and Lorentz-invariance constraints?

evidence.quote: However, there exist results which do not fit this picture and may suggest that the fourth (or, maybe, even the fifth) neutrino exists.
Other anomalies. Recent intense exploration of the field of neutrino oscillations revealed also a range of other anomalies which are currently being discussed and rechecked intensively.
All these very interesting anomalies currently await their confirmation in independent experiments.

These scenarios experience considerale difficulties with simultaneous explanation of the full set of the experimental data, though they cannot be totally excluded; it might happen that a certain combination of these possibilities is realized in Nature.

accepted.question_text: How should the Standard Model be extended so that neutrinos have nonzero masses and flavour mixing, given that the Standard Model contains only left-handed neutrinos and forbids a gauge-invariant renormalizable neutrino mass term, and how should the extension explain why neutrino masses are several orders of magnitude smaller than charged-fermion masses?

evidence.quote: By making use of the SM fields, it is impossible to construct a gauge invariant renormalizable interaction resulting in the neutrino mass, even after the electroweak symmetry breaking.
How can one modify SM to have massive neutrinos?
In any case, neutrinos are several orders of magnitude lighter than the charged fermions and a succesful theory of neutrino masses should be able to explain this fact (see also Sec. 4.3).

accepted.question_text: What physical mechanism generated the baryon asymmetry of the Universe, producing a matter-antimatter excess of order one unpaired quark per ten billion quark-antiquark pairs, when Standard Model electroweak baryogenesis fails because the required first-order electroweak phase transition would need an experimentally excluded light Higgs boson and CKM CP violation is insufficient?

evidence.quote: The ratio of the excess of quark number nq over the antiquark number, nq¯, is of order nq − nq¯ nq + nq¯ ∼ 10−10, that is a single “unpaired” quark was present for each ten billion quark-antiquark pairs.

However, it has been shown that the first-order electroweak phase transition in SM is possible only for the Higgs boson mass MH . 50 GeV which was excluded from direct searches long ago. Also, the amount of CP violation in the CKM matrix is insufficient.
A particular mechanism of generation of the baryon asymmetry is yet unknown (it should also explain the smallness of the asymmetry amount, ∼ 10−10).

accepted.question_text: What particles or composite objects constitute dark matter, with properties that make them almost stable over the lifetime of the Universe and only very weakly interacting with ordinary matter, given that astrophysical and cosmological observations require nonluminous non-baryonic mass and compact baryonic objects are excluded as the full explanation?

evidence.quote: These results, both by themselves and in combination with other results of quantitative cosmology (first of all those obtained from the analysis of the cosmic microwave background and the large-scale structure of the Universe, see e.g. [4]), point unequivocally to the existence of nonluminous matter.
These events have been indeed observed, but at a very low rate which allows for a firm exclusion of this explanation for dark matter [92].
We are forced to say that, probably, the dark matter consists of new, yet unknown, particles, so that its explanation requires to extend SM.

The dark-matter particles should be (almost) stable in order not to decay during the lifetime of the Universe (∼14 billion years). These particles should also interact with the ordinary matter only very weakly to avoid direct experimental detection (direct searches for the dark matter, which should exist everywhere, in particular in laboratories, last already for decades).

accepted.question_text: What is the physical nature of the dark energy that supplies about three-fourths of the critical energy density, does not cluster like matter, and drives the observed accelerated expansion of the Universe?

evidence.quote: At the same time, the estimates of the energy density related to matter contribute ∼ 0.25ρc, that is the remaining three fourths of the energy density of the Universe are due to something else.

This contribution, whose primary difference form the matter contribution is in the absence of clustering (that is of concentration in stars, galaxies, clusters etc.), carries a not fully successful name of “dark energy”.
The question about the nature of the dark energy is presently open.

accepted.question_text: If dark energy is vacuum energy or a cosmological constant, what mechanism cancels the huge vacuum-energy contributions expected from strong and electroweak particle physics while leaving the small observed nonzero scale Λ ∼ 10−3 eV, a scale not available among Standard Model parameters?

evidence.quote: The observed value of ρ corresponds to Λ ∼ 10−3 eV, while characteristic scales of the strong (ΛQCD ∼ 108 eV) and electroweak (v ∼ 1011 eV) interactions are many orders of magnitude higher.
One side of the problem (known for a long time as “the cosmologicalconstant problem”) is to explain how the contributions of all these interactions to the vacuum energy cancel.
On the other hand, the observed accelerated expansion of the Universe tells us that the cancellation is not complete and hence there is a new energetic scale in the Universe ∼ 10−3 eV.
The explanation of this scale is a task which cannot be completed within the frameworks of SM, where all parameters of the dimension of energy are orders of magnitude higher.

accepted.question_text: What particle-physics model, field, or mechanism caused early-universe inflation, what is the inflaton if a new scalar field drove the exponential expansion, and what caused inflation to stop rather than continue until the present?

evidence.quote: There are serious indications that, at an early stage of its evolution, the Universe experienced a period of intense exponential expansion, called inflation (see e.g. [78, 103].
It may be related to the presence of a new, absent in SM, scalar field, the inflaton.
For a particle physicist, at least two questions arise: first, what is the nature of the inflaton, and second, what was the reason for the inflation to stop and not to continue until now.

accepted.question_text: Can electroweak symmetry breaking be explained by a viable model that avoids or extends a fundamental Standard Model Higgs scalar—such as technicolor, extra-dimensional gauge-Higgs models, Higgsless boundary-condition models, or composite-Higgs dynamics—while preserving precision electroweak agreement and generating charged-fermion masses?

evidence.quote: One can see that the most preferable value of MH is already experimentally excluded! Clearly, this does not mean a catastrophe because a narrow range of slightly less preferable values are allowed, but it motivates theoretical physicists to think about possible alternative explanations of the electroweak symmetry breaking [109].
To construct an elegant and viable technicolor model is a task for future which will become relevant if the Higgs scalar will not be found at LHC.
Another shortcoming of this class of models is considerable arbitraryness in the choice of the boundary conditions, which are not derived from the model but are crucial for the electroweak breaking.
Description of these bound states requires a quantitative understanding of nonperturbative gauge dynamics.

accepted.question_text: What explains the origin, stability, and apparent desert of the gauge hierarchy: why the QCD and electroweak scales Λ_QCD ∼ 200 MeV and v ≈ 246 GeV are many orders of magnitude smaller than Planck, grand-unification, neutrino, or Peccei-Quinn scales; why electroweak radiative corrections do not require extreme fine tuning; and why no particles or interactions appear between the low and high scales?

evidence.quote: The gauge hierarchy problem (see also [2, 79, 113]) consists in the disproportionality of these scales: (ΛQCD, v) ≪ (MPl, MGUT, MPQ, Mν) and in a range of related questions which may be divided into three groups.
The origin of the hierarchy: why the scales of the strong and electroweak interactions are smaller than others by many orders of magnitude?
The stability of the hierarchy.

The third aspect of the same problem is related to the presumed absence of particles with masses (and of interactions with scales) between “small” (ΛQCD, v) and “large” (Mν, MGUT, MPl) energetic scales, see Fig. 13.

accepted.question_text: What underlying principle or model explains why the three generations of quarks and charged leptons have identical gauge interactions but masses and quark mixings with strong hierarchical patterns, while neutrino masses and leptonic mixing display a different and less suppressed hierarchy?

evidence.quote: The hierarchy of these masses is one of the biggest puzzles of particle physics.
The hierarchical structure appears both in the diagonal elements (which differ by orders of magnitude) and in the off-diagonal ones (the mixing is suppressed).
A modern theory which succesfully explains the fermion masses should motivate both hierarchical structures and explain why they are different.
Meanwhile, even without the neutrino sector, the intergeneration mass hierarchy is very difficult to explain.

accepted.question_text: How can QCD at strong coupling be solved from first principles so that confinement, the formation of colorless hadrons from quarks and gluons, and low- and intermediate-energy hadron properties and interactions are derived quantitatively rather than modeled phenomenologically?

evidence.quote: In this section, we discuss the question about the practical applicability of the quantum field theory to the description of interactions with large coupling constants, and in particular to the low-energy limit of QCD.

Before proceeding to the discussion of these achievements, let us note that despite a significant progress, the problem of description of strong interactions at low energies in terms of QCD is not solved, so the development of the corresponding methods remains one of the basic tasks of the quantum field theory.

To understand the nature of confinement and to describe properties of hadrons from the first principles (and, in the end, to answer whether QCD is applicable to the description of hadrons), one require the methods of the field theory which do not make use of the expansion in powers of the coupling constants (non-perturbative methods).

accepted.question_text: At what momentum-transfer scales does perturbative QCD become reliable for exclusive hadronic observables such as pion form factors, and why do measurements up to roughly 2–4 GeV fail to show a clear approach to perturbative predictions?

evidence.quote: A number of recent experimental results related to the measurement of the form factors of π mesons question the applicability of perturbative methods at considerably higher momentum transfer (a few GeV).
Up to the energy scale ∼ 2 GeV, there are no signs of approaching the perturbative regime.
One may see that the perturbative QCD experience some difficulties in explaining the experiment at the momentum transfer . 4 GeV.

accepted.question_text: How can effective theories written in observable hadron degrees of freedom be rigorously justified as low-energy limits of QCD rather than treated as phenomenological models whose connection to the underlying quark-and-gluon theory remains unproven?

evidence.quote: Approaches to nonperturbative description of QCD may be divided into two classes: (1) calculations in QCD beyond the perturbation theory (the only available method here is the numerical calculation of the functional integral on the lattice) and (2) construction of an effective theory in terms of degrees of freedom which correspond to obsevrable particles.
In the latter case the main unsolved question is, as a rule, to justify the connection of the effective theory to QCD.

accepted.question_text: Can one prove that the continuum limit of lattice QCD exists, is independent of the way the lattice size tends to infinity and the lattice spacing tends to zero, and coincides with continuum QCD despite theoretical differences such as the treatment of instantons and chiral fermions?

evidence.quote: It is an open theoretical question to prove that the continuum limit of a lattice field theory exists (that is the physical results do not depend on the way in which the lattice size tends to infinity and the lattice step tends to zero) and coincides with QCD.

At the same time, theoretically, the difference between the lattice and continuum theories is large; for instance, topologically stable in the continuum theory configurations, instantons, which determine the structure of vacuum in nonabelian gauge theories, are not always stable on the lattice; the lattice description of chiral fermions (automatic in a continuum theory) requires complicated constructions etc.

accepted.question_text: Can a weakly coupled dual or holographic theory for real QCD be constructed and proven, so that low- and intermediate-energy strong dynamics can be calculated from a dual theory rather than chosen through partly arbitrary five-dimensional effective models?
accepted.context_brief: Dual and holographic descriptions of QCD

evidence.quote: Note that the theory dual to QCD has not been constructed up to now.
A disadvantage of the method is that the duality between QCD and the five-dimensional effective theory is not proven.
As a result, the choice of the latter is somewhat arbitrary.
One may hope that in the future, a lowenergy effective theory for QCD might be derived in the frameworks of this approach.
